'''John Tiplady Carrodus''' (1836–1895) was an English [[violin]]ist.

==Life==
[[File:Family grave of John Tiplady Carrodus in Highgate Cemetery.jpg|thumb|left|Family grave of John Tiplady Carrodus in [[Highgate Cemetery]]]]
Carrodus was born on 20 January 1836, at [[Keighley]], in the [[West Riding of Yorkshire]]. He took violin lessons from his father Thomas Carrodus, who was a barber and music-seller.<ref name="auto">{{cite book |last= Orel |first= Harold |author-link= |date= 3 December 1996|title= The Brontës: Interviews and Recollections| url= https://books.google.com/books?id=0eGMnGqeMWUC|access-date= 27 March 2022|location= Iowa City | publisher= University of Iowa Press| page= 203| isbn= 978-0-877-45537-0}}</ref> He made his first appearance as a violinist at the age of nine, and before the London public four years later.<ref name="auto1">{{cite book |last= Boden |first= Anthony |author-link= |date= 16 June 2017|title= The Three Choirs Festival: A History| url= https://books.google.com/books?id=E7Q4DwAAQBAJ|access-date= 27 March 2022|location= Woodbridge, Suffolk, England | publisher= Boydell & Brewer | page= 86| isbn= 978-1-783-27209-9}}</ref> He had the advantage of studying between the ages of twelve and eighteen at [[Stuttgart]], with [[Bernhard Molique]].{{sfn|Chisholm|1911}}<ref name="auto1"/> He also "became a 'follower of [[Louis Spohr|Spohr]]', who expressed his admiration for the Englishman's playing."<ref name="auto2">{{cite book |last= Golby|first= David  |author-link= |date= 17 June 2016|title= Instrumental Teaching in Nineteenth-Century Britain | url= https://books.google.com/books?id=vRpqDAAAQBAJ|access-date= 27 March 2022|location= Oxon | publisher= Routledge| page=205| isbn= 978-1-317-22072-5}}</ref>

On his return to Britain in 1853 [[Michael Costa (conductor)|Sir Michael Costa]] got him engagements in the leading orchestras. He was a member of the [[Royal Opera House|Covent Garden opera]] orchestra from 1855.<ref name="auto3">{{cite book |last= Katz |first= Mark  |author-link= |date= 9 February 2006|title= The Violin: A Research and Information Guide | url= https://books.google.com/books?id=qJlsBgAAQBAJ|access-date= 27 March 2022|location= Oxon | publisher= Routledge| page=302| isbn= 978-1-135-57696-7 }}</ref> He made his debut as a solo player at a concert given on 22 April 1863 by the [[Musical Society of London]], and succeeded [[Prosper Sainton]] as leader at Covent Garden in 1869.{{sfn|Chisholm|1911}} He led the Covent Garden orchestra for twenty-five years.<ref name="auto4">{{cite book |last= Gilbert|first= Susie   |author-link= |date= 3 March 2011|title= Opera for Everybody: The Story of English National Opera | url= https://books.google.com/books?id=3Q-4GoEnnYEC|access-date= 27 March 2022|location= London | publisher= Faber & Faber  | page=13| isbn= 978-0-571-26865-8}}</ref>  He also took over from Sainton as the Leader of the Three Choirs Festival orchestra in 1882.<ref name="auto1"/>

He taught at the [[National Training School of Music]], the Croydon Conservatoire of Music, the Guildhall School of Music, the Royal Academy of Music, and Trinity College, London. He has the distinction of being  the first president of the College of Violinists.<ref name="auto2"/><ref name="auto3"/><ref name="auto4"/> He was an early proponent of the violin recital.<ref name="auto3"/> His concert at St James's Hall on 20 January 1881, which included the  works of Molique and Spohr, is "widely recognized as the first public violin recital."<ref name="auto2"/>

For many years, Carrodus had led the orchestra of the Philharmonic Society<ref name="auto1"/><ref>{{cite book |last= Birkin |first= Kenneth |author-link= |date= 7 July 2011|title= Hans Von Bülow: A Life for Music| url= https://books.google.com/books?id=33VWI2ONlP8C|access-date= 27 March 2022|location= Cambridge | publisher= Cambridge University Press| page= 260| isbn= 978-1-107-00586-0}}</ref> and those of the great provincial festivals. The coveted ''Carrodus'' violin, made by [[Giuseppe Guarneri|Guarneri]] in 1743, was said to have belonged to Carrodus.

Carrodus was constantly striving "for improving the standard of string playing in English orchestras." He was famous for setting extremely high standards in his own playing and in that of his pupils.<ref>{{cite book |last= Schafer|first= Elizabeth   |author-link= |date= 1 October 2007|title= Lilian Baylis: A Biography| url= https://books.google.com/books?id=U4Y6Jyc0vSAC|access-date= 27 March 2022|location= Hatfield, United Kingdom | publisher= University of Hertfordshire Press| page=13| isbn= 978-1-902-80664-8}}</ref> [[Lilian Baylis]] was one of his notable students. He taught her violin at  the Royal Academy of Music.<ref name="auto4"/>

In addition to editions of the treatises of Loder  and Spohr, Carrodus published his own "Chats to violin students on how to study the violin."<ref name="auto2"/> He published two violin solos and a {{lang|fr|Morceau de salon}}, and was a very successful teacher.{{sfn|Chisholm|1911}} <ref>{{cite book |last= Zon|first= Bennett   |author-link= |date= 29 April 2016|title= Music and Performance Culture in Nineteenth-Century Britain: Essays in Honour of Nicholas Temperley| url= https://books.google.com/books?id=MIYWDAAAQBAJ|access-date= 27 March 2022|location= Oxon | publisher= Routledge | page=18| isbn= 978-1-317-09238-4}}</ref> He edited a popular six-volume edition of violin duets for Pitman's Sixpenny Musical Library.<ref name="auto"/>

He died at [[Hampstead]], [[London]] on 13 July 1895{{sfn|Chisholm|1911}} and was buried in a family grave on the eastern side of [[Highgate Cemetery]].
